choices.text: The student is right - the formula shows the two atoms joined as a molecule
Salt is a giant ionic lattice of separate ions, and the formula gives only the ratio
Salt is made of molecules, but each molecule has millions of atoms
Salt is a metal, so its atoms sit in a sea of electrons

questions.feedback: If you pictured a molecule, that is the trap: Table salt is made of NaCl molecules. Reteach point: Salt is a giant ionic lattice: NaCl just gives the ratio, there are no separate NaCl molecules. Every ion is held by its neighbours in one repeating pattern.
questions.misconception: Table salt is made of NaCl molecules.
questions.prompt: A student says a grain of salt is one huge NaCl molecule. What is the best correction?

questions.answer: Magnesium loses its 2 outer electrons to form a positive magnesium ion, and oxygen gains 2 electrons to form a negative oxide ion. The bond is ionic.
questions.feedback: A strong answer moves the electrons first, then names the ions: losing electrons makes a positive ion, gaining makes a negative one. If you wrote that the atoms share electrons, that describes covalent bonding instead.
questions.prompt: Magnesium has electron arrangement 2,8,2 and oxygen has 2,6. State the ions formed when they bond, and the type of bond.

choices.text: Sodium chloride, a lattice of ions
Copper, a lattice of ions in a sea of electrons
Water, molecules with shared pairs of electrons
Magnesium oxide, ions formed by electron transfer

questions.feedback: Water is the covalent one: its atoms share pairs of electrons and form separate molecules. Sodium chloride and magnesium oxide are ionic, and copper is metallic.
questions.prompt: Which substance is held together by covalent bonding?

questions.answer: Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice, and every ion is held by strong attractions to the oppositely charged ions all around it. A huge amount of energy is needed to break down the whole lattice, so its melting point is very high.
questions.feedback: A strong answer names the giant lattice and the attractions in every direction. An answer about breaking molecules apart has fallen for the molecule picture - there are no molecules in the lattice to separate.
questions.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain why sodium chloride has a very high melting point.
